locator: 5.1 Lactic Acidosis; 5.2 Vitamin B12 Deficiency; 5.3 Hypoglycemia; 6 Adverse Reactions
paragraph: Metformin commonly causes diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, gas and abdominal discomfort, while prolonged treatment can lower vitamin B12 concentrations. Its boxed warning concerns lactic acidosis, a potentially fatal buildup of acid associated with metformin accumulation. Kidney impairment is particularly important because the drug is eliminated through the kidneys; hypoxic illness, liver impairment, excessive alcohol use and certain interacting medicines add risk. The label also identifies surgery, restricted food or fluid intake and some iodinated-contrast procedures as situations requiring a separate interruption and kidney-function assessment. Metformin alone does not normally stimulate insulin release, but hypoglycemia becomes more likely when it is combined with insulin or an insulin secretagogue. Periodic kidney assessment, blood counts and vitamin B12 assessment address different hazards. These precautions concern the labeled oral product and remain relevant when research proposes using the same medicine outside diabetes.

locator: 2.3 Renal Impairment; 2.4 Iodinated Contrast; 4 Contraindications; 5.1
paragraph: The tablet label lists three formal contraindications: severe kidney impairment, hypersensitivity to metformin, and acute or chronic metabolic acidosis, including diabetic ketoacidosis. Severe kidney impairment is defined as an estimated glomerular filtration rate below 30 mL/min/1.73 m². A different threshold governs starting treatment: initiation is not recommended when this estimate is between 30 and 45. If kidney function subsequently falls below 45 during established treatment, the label calls for reassessing the balance of benefit and risk, rather than treating that threshold as identical to the absolute contraindication below 30. Iodinated contrast, hypoxic illness, excessive alcohol consumption and liver impairment introduce additional precautions and interruption decisions. Those situations must remain distinct from the formal contraindication list. The restrictions also concern the actual patient and formulation; eligibility for one repurposing trial does not establish that every other patient can safely receive metformin.

locator: 7 Drug Interactions; 5.1 Lactic Acidosis; 5.3 Hypoglycemia
paragraph: Metformin interactions can increase drug exposure, worsen susceptibility to acidosis, or increase hypoglycemia when another glucose-lowering medicine is present. Drugs that reduce renal clearance, including cimetidine, dolutegravir and ranolazine, can increase metformin accumulation. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors such as topiramate can lower bicarbonate and contribute to metabolic acidosis, creating a different interaction pathway. Excessive alcohol intake affects lactate metabolism and is another concern in the lactic-acidosis warning. Insulin and sulfonylureas can increase hypoglycemia risk even though metformin itself does not stimulate insulin secretion. Other medicines can raise blood glucose and affect diabetes control, so stopping or starting them can also change the clinical context. These categories are not interchangeable: an exposure interaction is different from additive glucose lowering or an acid-base effect. The label describes them alongside kidney-function and acute-illness precautions, rather than providing a blanket clearance for any proposed repurposing combination.

locator: 2.1 Adult Dosage; 2.2 Pediatric Dosage; 2.3 Renal Impairment
paragraph: The immediate-release tablet label describes administration with meals and gradual increases according to tolerability and glucose control, rather than one starting schedule for every patient. Its adult maximum is different from its pediatric maximum, and kidney-function restrictions apply before treatment and during follow-up. Those labeled diabetes schedules must be kept separate from the short prevention courses and longer research regimens summarized above.

locator: Immediate-release and extended-release labels: Dosage and Administration; Dosage Forms; FDA Generic Drug Facts
paragraph: Metformin product identity includes its release formulation, tablet strength and intended dosing schedule. The immediate-release and extended-release labels describe different administration patterns; an extended-release tablet is designed to release its contents over time and is swallowed whole, rather than crushed or chewed. An immediate-release regimen used in a trial therefore cannot be converted into an extended-release research regimen simply by matching the total milligrams. The two products also have their own dose-increase instructions and labeled limits. FDA-approved generic products must meet the relevant requirements for the reference product, including active ingredient, strength, dosage form, route and bioequivalence. That regulatory comparison concerns a specified reference formulation. It does not establish that every release formulation, compounded preparation or differently scheduled product reproduces the exposure or clinical findings of a particular repurposing trial.

locator: Boxed Warning; 5 Warnings and Precautions; 6 Adverse Reactions
paragraph: Nirmatrelvir with ritonavir has a safety profile dominated by ritonavir's strong inhibition of CYP3A, an enzyme involved in clearing many medicines. An interacting drug can accumulate enough to cause severe, life-threatening or fatal effects, so the label's boxed warning makes medication review central to treatment. Common reported reactions include altered taste and diarrhea, but these are distinct from serious hypersensitivity reactions and the hepatic risks associated with ritonavir. Kidney impairment also changes the appropriate dose pack and schedule because nirmatrelvir exposure rises when renal clearance is reduced. Severe liver impairment is a separate setting in which the product is not recommended. The labeled treatment is a short course for eligible adults with acute COVID-19; that defined exposure does not establish the safety or effectiveness of prolonged courses, different combinations or treatment of established Long COVID.

locator: 4 Contraindications; 5.1 Significant Drug Interactions; 2 Renal Impairment
paragraph: The product is contraindicated after a clinically significant hypersensitivity reaction to nirmatrelvir, ritonavir or another component. Its other major contraindications concern specified interacting medicines. One group consists of drugs primarily metabolized by CYP3A for which increased concentrations can cause serious or life-threatening reactions. Another consists of potent CYP3A inducers that can reduce antiviral concentrations enough to compromise the response and permit resistance. Stopping an inducer immediately before antiviral treatment may not remove its effect because enzyme induction can persist. These restrictions are different from dose adjustment for kidney impairment and from the recommendation against use in severe liver impairment. The actual interacting medicine, its clearance pathway and the consequences of changing its exposure determine the restriction. A general statement that a patient takes several medicines cannot replace the product-specific interaction assessment required by the label.

locator: 4 Contraindications; 7 Drug Interactions; 5.1
paragraph: Ritonavir is included to inhibit metabolism and sustain nirmatrelvir exposure, but that same pharmacology changes the exposure of many other medicines. The label distinguishes combinations that are contraindicated from those requiring interruption, dose adjustment or additional monitoring. Clinically important examples span antiarrhythmics, anticoagulants, anticonvulsants, lipid-lowering medicines and immunosuppressants, with different instructions for individual agents. Strong enzyme inducers create the opposite problem by lowering antiviral concentrations, and their effects may persist after withdrawal. This is why a recently stopped drug can still matter. Kidney function, the competing medicine's therapeutic range and the feasibility of changing its regimen all affect interpretation. These interactions cannot be summarized as a single drug-class prohibition or assumed absent because the antiviral course lasts only five days. The source is the co-packaged nirmatrelvir/ritonavir product label, not a study of unrestricted repurposing combinations.

locator: 2 Dosage and Administration; 3 Dosage Forms and Strengths; 16 How Supplied
paragraph: The marketed product contains separate nirmatrelvir and ritonavir tablets packaged together, rather than one tablet containing both active ingredients. Nirmatrelvir supplies the antiviral action, while ritonavir changes its exposure through metabolic inhibition. The packaging therefore helps identify both components and their scheduled administration. The cited label describes different dose packs for different levels of kidney function; the contents and instructions of one pack cannot be assumed to apply to every patient. Tablet identity, tablet count and the actual renal regimen matter alongside the product name. These product-specific distinctions also limit interpretation of repurposing research: a study of the combination does not test nirmatrelvir alone, ritonavir alone, an arbitrary mixture of antiviral medicines or a longer unstudied course. Matching the printed strength of one component would not reproduce the complete labeled exposure and schedule.

locator: Boxed Warning; Warnings: Hepatic Effects, Cardiac Disease, Pseudoaldosteronism; Adverse Reactions
paragraph: Itraconazole can cause gastrointestinal symptoms, but its most consequential hazards concern the heart, liver and interacting medicines. The capsule label describes a negative effect on cardiac contraction and reports of congestive heart failure, including cases outside treatment of fungal nail infection. Serious liver injury, including liver failure and death, has also been reported, sometimes early in treatment and without previously recognized liver disease. Another reported complication is pseudoaldosteronism, which can present with higher blood pressure and low potassium. Some interactions increase other drugs' concentrations enough to cause dangerous rhythm disturbances, while other combinations add cardiac or hepatic stress. The indication-specific cardiac restrictions, formal drug-interaction contraindications and broader precautions have different meanings. Cancer combinations therefore require interpretation of the complete regimen and the actual capsule formulation; a small trial's activity signal does not remove these established product risks.

locator: Contraindications; Warnings: Cardiac Disease; Boxed Warning
paragraph: Itraconazole capsules are contraindicated for fungal nail infection in patients with ventricular dysfunction, including congestive heart failure or a history of heart failure. The same label treats other indications differently: use in ventricular dysfunction requires a benefit that clearly outweighs the risk. Pregnancy and planned pregnancy are also explicit restrictions for treatment of fungal nail infection. Hypersensitivity to itraconazole is a separate contraindication that is not limited to that indication. In addition, numerous named co-medications are contraindicated because their concentrations or effects can increase dangerously. Examples include simvastatin, lovastatin and oral midazolam; other restrictions depend on kidney or liver function or a specific treatment phase. These distinctions matter when discussing repurposing. An indication-specific restriction cannot simply be presented as a universal ban, while its narrower wording also cannot be interpreted as reassurance that a different investigational use is safe.

locator: Precautions: Drug Interactions; Clinical Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetics; Boxed Warning
paragraph: Itraconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and can substantially increase exposure to medicines cleared through that pathway. The capsule label lists contraindicated combinations, combinations that are not recommended, and combinations requiring caution or monitoring; these are distinct levels of restriction. Simvastatin, lovastatin and oral midazolam are among the contraindicated examples. Calcium-channel blockers can create both a pharmacokinetic interaction and an additional cardiac effect, with specific agents expressly contraindicated. Acid-suppressing medicines introduce a different problem: reduced stomach acidity can lower absorption of the capsules and reduce itraconazole exposure. Enzyme-inducing drugs can also lower its concentrations. Consequently, a combination can be problematic through excessive exposure, inadequate exposure or added organ toxicity. These mechanisms require interpretation of the individual drugs and formulation, rather than a general claim that all antifungals or all cancer regimens have the same interaction profile.

locator: Dosage and Administration; Clinical Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetics; Warnings: Interchangeability
paragraph: Itraconazole dosing depends on the infection, product and intended treatment schedule. The capsule label describes different regimens for systemic fungal infections and fungal nail infection, including schedules with different daily doses and durations. Capsules are taken immediately after a full meal because food affects absorption. Reduced gastric acidity can lower their uptake, and the product label discusses this separately from dose selection. The oral solution produces different exposure at the same nominal dose and is not interchangeable with the capsules. Those distinctions are important when reading cancer-repurposing reports, which can use their own schedules and co-treatments rather than a labeled antifungal regimen. Neither a capsule dose used for one infection nor a dose reported in a small oncology trial establishes a general anticancer schedule. Formulation, administration conditions, interacting medicines and the exact trial population must remain attached to any reported dose.

locator: Description; Clinical Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetics; Warnings: Interchangeability; How Supplied
paragraph: The cited product is a 100-mg itraconazole capsule containing drug-coated pellets, and its formulation is relevant to absorption. The capsule label describes greater absorption immediately after a full meal and lower absorption when stomach acidity is reduced. It also explicitly states that capsules and oral solution should not be used interchangeably: the solution gives greater drug exposure at the same nominal dose, and local mucosal exposure can differ. Evidence for the oral solution in oral or esophageal candidiasis therefore does not automatically establish the same result for capsules. These are product and exposure distinctions, rather than cosmetic differences between packaging. When comparing repurposing studies, the drug name and milligram amount alone do not identify the tested intervention. The formulation, meal conditions, acid-suppressing medicines and accompanying treatment need to match before results can be interpreted as evidence for the same regimen.

locator: Warnings: Vulnerability to Opioid Overdose, Precipitated Withdrawal, Hepatotoxicity; Adverse Reactions
paragraph: Naltrexone can cause nausea, headache, dizziness, fatigue and other adverse reactions, but its opioid-antagonist action creates several distinctive serious hazards. Starting it while a person remains dependent on opioids can precipitate abrupt withdrawal severe enough to require hospital or intensive care. Attempting to overcome its receptor blockade with large opioid doses can cause fatal overdose. After treatment stops and the blockade wanes, reduced opioid tolerance can also make previously tolerated amounts dangerous. The tablet label separately describes hepatitis and clinically significant liver dysfunction, as well as reports of depression or suicidal thinking that require attention to the clinical context. Low-dose repurposing schedules do not establish that these pharmacological concerns disappear. Opioid exposure, the actual dose and formulation, liver status and the availability of an appropriate pain-management plan all remain relevant to interpreting an individual study's safety findings.

locator: Contraindications; Warnings: Precipitated Withdrawal; Precautions
paragraph: The oral naltrexone label contraindicates treatment in patients receiving opioid analgesics, those currently dependent on opioids, and those in acute opioid withdrawal. Dependence includes maintenance treatment with an opioid agonist such as methadone or a partial agonist such as buprenorphine. A positive opioid urine screen or a failed naloxone challenge is another stated contraindication, and sensitivity to naltrexone or a product component is listed separately. These restrictions follow from receptor blockade and the possibility of severe precipitated withdrawal. The label also explains that a negative screen or challenge does not completely exclude that possibility, particularly during transitions from certain maintenance treatments. A low-dose research regimen is therefore not a general exception to opioid-related assessment. Formal contraindications, liver-related warnings and the trial's own eligibility criteria describe different boundaries and should not be merged into one undifferentiated exclusion list.

locator: Precautions: Drug Interactions; Warnings: Vulnerability to Overdose; Emergency Pain Management
paragraph: Naltrexone can block the effects of opioid-containing medicines, including some analgesics, cough preparations and antidiarrheal products. This is a pharmacodynamic interaction at opioid receptors, rather than simply competition for the same metabolic enzyme. The label describes special difficulties when emergency opioid analgesia is required: larger opioid amounts may be needed, but respiratory depression can then be deeper and more prolonged. It also warns that attempts to overcome the blockade outside an appropriate medical setting can be fatal. Evidence for interactions with non-opioid drugs is less complete; the tablet label states that dedicated studies of many such combinations have not been performed. It specifically discusses the uncertain safety of concurrent disulfiram and reports of lethargy or somnolence with thioridazine. These limits mean that absence of a listed interaction is not a completed assessment of an arbitrary repurposing combination.

locator: Description; Indications and Usage; Dosage and Administration; How Supplied
paragraph: The cited naltrexone product is an oral 50-mg tablet with a defined strength, formulation and addiction-treatment labeling. That product identity should remain attached to discussions of its pharmacology and restrictions. Repurposing schedules discussed elsewhere on this page can involve smaller doses and different treatment goals; the tablet label does not itself establish efficacy or product equivalence for those schedules. A nominal milligram amount also does not describe how a different preparation was manufactured, measured or evaluated. The labeled tablet's use to block opioid effects must not be confused with proof that every preparation described as low-dose naltrexone has been tested against the same reference product. Interpreting a study therefore requires the actual oral product, strength and administered regimen, together with its clinical evidence. The label supplies product and safety context, while the relevant trial supplies the evidence for its specific investigated use.

locator: 5 Warnings and Precautions; 6 Adverse Reactions; 8.6 Renal Impairment
paragraph: Pramipexole can cause nausea, sleepiness, dizziness and orthostatic hypotension, but its warnings extend beyond those common symptoms. Patients have reported suddenly falling asleep during ordinary activities, sometimes without an obvious warning of drowsiness. Hallucinations, psychotic-like behavior and impulse-control problems, including compulsive gambling, spending or sexual behavior, are additional concerns with dopamine-agonist treatment. Kidney impairment increases exposure because renal elimination is important, while the indication and dose schedule affect tolerability. The label also describes withdrawal-related symptoms and the need to distinguish discontinuation effects from the underlying disorder. These issues are relevant to depression research as well as the established movement-disorder uses: a change in the treatment goal does not change the medicine's receptor activity. Trial safety findings must therefore retain their actual dose, population, co-medications and follow-up rather than becoming a general claim that psychiatric or repurposed use is well tolerated.

locator: 4 Contraindications; 5 Warnings and Precautions; 2 Dosage and Administration; 8.6
paragraph: The cited pramipexole tablet label lists no formal contraindications. That statement must remain separate from its substantial warnings and dose restrictions. The label describes sudden sleep episodes, symptomatic orthostatic hypotension, hallucinations and psychotic-like behavior, and urges assessment of impulse-control or compulsive behaviors. Reduced kidney function can require a different dose or titration schedule because the drug is predominantly cleared through the kidneys. Co-administered sedatives and other dopamine-active medicines also affect the clinical context. These are not converted into formal contraindications simply because they are consequential, and absence of a formal contraindication is not proof that a particular person or investigational indication has been assessed. The distinction is especially important when reading treatment-resistant-depression studies: their screening rules and exclusions characterize the people studied, while the product label describes a different set of pharmacological precautions.

locator: 7 Drug Interactions; 12.3 Pharmacokinetics: Drug Interactions; 5.1 Somnolence
paragraph: Pramipexole interactions involve renal elimination, dopamine signaling and additive effects on alertness or blood pressure. Cimetidine inhibits renal tubular secretion and increases pramipexole exposure; other medicines using the same renal transport pathway may also matter. Dopamine antagonists can oppose the intended receptor action, making the pharmacological relationship different from an interaction that raises blood concentrations. Alcohol and sedating medicines are relevant to the warning about sleepiness and sudden sleep episodes. In Parkinson's disease, co-treatment with levodopa can also affect adverse effects such as dyskinesia and the required clinical adjustments. These mechanisms should be considered separately instead of assigning all combinations the same risk or severity. The cited label supports interpretation of the oral tablet, while a psychiatric repurposing trial tests only its stated regimen and co-medications. An untested drug combination cannot be cleared by assuming that pramipexole has little hepatic metabolism.

locator: 3 Dosage Forms and Strengths; 2 Dosage and Administration; 12.3 Pharmacokinetics; 16 How Supplied
paragraph: The cited pramipexole product is a conventional oral tablet, supplied in defined strengths and described using pramipexole dihydrochloride. Product identity includes that salt designation and the release formulation, not simply the shortened drug name. The label uses different dosing schedules for Parkinson's disease and restless legs syndrome and adjusts dosing for kidney function. Those instructions define the evaluated product context; they do not establish a schedule for every investigated psychiatric use. When comparing studies or preparations, the actual tablet strength, formulation and administered frequency therefore need to be retained. A differently released or differently expressed product cannot be treated as the same intervention merely because its packaging also says pramipexole. The clinical results on this page concern their reported regimens, and the product label supplies the distinct formulation, pharmacokinetic and safety information needed to interpret those regimens.

locator: 2 Dosage and Administration; 3 Dosage Forms; Clinical Pharmacology: Pharmacokinetics
paragraph: Sirolimus product identity includes formulation, strength and the conditions under which blood concentrations are measured. The cited tablet label supplies several strengths and describes monitoring of whole-blood sirolimus concentrations because exposure varies with administration conditions, metabolism and interacting medicines. It also discusses the relationship between tablets and oral solution, rather than assuming that equal nominal amounts always establish equivalent exposure. Consistency in taking the product with or without food is relevant to that pharmacokinetic interpretation. These details matter when transplant regimens, lymphangioleiomyomatosis treatment and experimental studies use different schedules or accompanying drugs. A laboratory or animal experiment with rapamycin does not test the quality or clinical exposure of every marketed or compounded preparation. The actual formulation, dose schedule, food conditions and measured concentrations need to remain attached to each study before its findings can be compared with the labeled oral product.
